      <content name="title"><span class="qt1">Itching</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0">Pruritus</span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt1">itching</span>?<p><span class="qt1">Itching</span> is an irritating sensation that makes you want to scratch your skin. Sometimes it can feel like pain, but it is different. Often, you feel itchy in one area in your body, but sometimes you may feel <span class="qt1">itching</span> all over. Along with the <span class="qt1">itching</span>, you may also have a rash or hives.</p>What causes <span class="qt1">itching</span>?<p><span class="qt1">Itching</span> is a symptom of many health conditions. Some common causes are:</p><ul><li>Allergic reactions to food, insect bites, pollen, and medicines</li><li>Skin conditions such as eczema, psoriasis, and dry skin</li><li>Irritating chemicals, cosmetics, and other substances</li><li>Parasites such as pinworms, scabies, head and body lice</li><li>Pregnancy</li><li>Liver, kidney, or thyroid diseases</li><li>Certain cancers or cancer treatments</li><li>Diseases that can affect the nervous system, such as diabetes and shingles</li></ul>What are the treatments for <span class="qt1">itching</span>?<p>Most <span class="qt1">itching</span> is not serious. To feel better, you could try:</p><ul><li>Applying cold compresses</li><li>Using moisturizing lotions</li><li>Taking lukewarm or oatmeal baths</li><li>Using over-the-counter hydrocortisone cream or antihistamines</li><li>Avoiding scratching, wearing irritating fabrics, and exposure to high heat and humidity</li></ul><p>Contact your health care provider if your <span class="qt1">itching</span> is severe, does not go away after a few weeks, or does not have an apparent cause. You may need other treatments, such as medicines or light therapy. If you have an underlying disease that is causing the <span class="qt1">itching</span>, treating that disease may help.</p></content>

      <content name="title">Anal Disorders</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0">Pruritus</span> Ani</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Anorectal diseases</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is the anus?<p>Your anus is the opening at the end of your large intestine. It is where stool (poop) leaves your body.</p>What are anal disorders?<p>Problems with the anus are common. They include:</p><ul><li>Hemorrhoids</li><li>Abscesses</li><li>Fissures, small cracks or tears in the lining of your anus</li><li>Anorectal fistula, an abnormal tunnel from your anus or rectum to the skin surface</li><li>Anal <span class="qt1">itching</span> (<span class="qt0">pruritus</span> ani)</li><li>Cancer</li></ul>What are the symptoms of anal disorders?<p>Your symptoms will depend on which disorder you have. But some of the more common symptoms may include:</p><ul><li>Bleeding</li><li>Discharge</li><li><span class="qt1">Itching</span></li><li>Pain</li><li>Swelling</li></ul>How are anal disorders diagnosed?<p>To make a diagnosis, your health care provider will ask about your symptoms and medical history. Depending upon your symptoms, your provider may:</p><ul><li>Check the skin around your anus for anything that looks abnormal.</li><li>Perform a digital rectal exam (DRE).  For this exam, your provider inserts a lubricated, gloved finger into the lower part of your rectum to feel for lumps or anything unusual.</li><li>Order tests, such as an anoscopy.</li></ul><p>You may be embarrassed to talk about your anal troubles. But it's important to let your provider know about your symptoms, especially if you have pain or bleeding. The more details you can give about your problem, the better your provider can help you.</p>How are anal disorders treated?<p>Treatments vary, depending on the condition you have.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases </p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/vulvardisorders.html">
      <content name="title">Vulvar Disorders</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Vulvodynia</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What are vulvar disorders?<p>The vulva is the outer part of the female genitals. This includes the clitoris, vaginal lips, and the opening to the vagina. A vulvar disorder is a health problem that affects your vulva. These problems may cause pain, <span class="qt1">itching</span>, or skin changes of the vulva. Treatment depends on the cause.</p><p>Common vulvar disorders include:</p><ul><li>Vaginitis or vulvovaginitis, which is swelling or infection of the vulva and vagina</li><li><span class="qt1">Itching</span> (<span class="qt0">pruritus</span> vulvae) or skin rashes due to allergies or irritation</li><li>Vulvar cancer</li><li>Vulvodynia, which is long-lasting vulvar pain without a known medical cause</li><li>Lichen sclerosus, which is thin, itchy, white patches of skin on the vulva</li><li>Vulvitis, which is inflammation of the vulva</li><li>Labial adhesions, which is when the folds of skin around the vaginal opening stick together (most common in young girls)</li></ul>Who is more likely to develop vulvar disorders?<p>Vulvar disorders can affect women and girls of any age, but certain factors may raise their risk. This includes those:</p><ul><li>Going through or past menopause. Lower estrogen can lead to thinning skin and conditions like lichen sclerosus.</li><li>Having certain skin conditions or allergies, which can raise your risk of vulvar skin problems.</li></ul>What are the symptoms of vulvar disorders?<p>Symptoms depend on the specific disorder. Common symptoms may include:</p><ul><li>Redness or swelling</li><li><span class="qt1">Itching</span> or burning</li><li>Pain, especially during sex or urination (peeing)</li><li>Cracks, sores, or thickened patches of skin</li><li>Changes in skin color, such as lighter, darker, or white patches</li><li>Lumps, growths, or sores that don't heal</li><li>Vaginal bleeding that isn't related to your menstrual period</li></ul><p>Talk to your health care provider if symptoms last more than a few days, you notice a new lump or a sore that won't heal, or you have vaginal bleeding that's not normal for you.</p>How are vulvar disorders diagnosed?<p>Early diagnosis may make most vulvar disorders easier to treat. To diagnose a vulvar disorder, your provider may:</p><ul><li>Ask about your health history and symptoms</li><li>Do a pelvic exam</li><li>Test for HPV or do a Pap test</li><li>Use a magnifying tool (colposcope) to look closely at the skin of your vulva</li></ul>What are the treatments for vulvar disorders?<p>Treatment depends on the cause. It may include:</p><ul><li>Medicines, such as antibiotics, antifungals, or other medicines</li><li>Creams or steroid ointments for irritation or allergic reactions</li><li>Pelvic floor physical therapy (to stretch and ease vulvodynia pain), nerve blocks or medicines, counseling, or a combination of these treatments</li></ul>Can vulvar disorders be prevented?<p>Not all vulvar disorders can be prevented, but you can lower your risk by:</p><ul><li>Getting the HPV vaccine to help prevent infections linked to vulvar cancer</li><li>Not smoking</li><li>Practicing good hygiene, such as wearing cotton underwear and avoiding scented soaps or douches</li><li>Getting regular checkups, including pelvic exams, so problems can be found early</li></ul></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/anaphylaxis.html">
      <content name="title">Anaphylaxis</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Anaphylactic shock</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Anaphylaxis is a serious allergic reaction. It can begin very quickly, and symptoms may be life-threatening. The most common causes are reactions to foods (especially peanuts), medications, and stinging insects. Other causes include exercise and exposure to latex. Sometimes no cause can be found.</p><p>It can affect many organs:</p><ul><li>Skin - <span class="qt1">itching</span>, hives, redness, swelling</li><li>Nose - sneezing, stuffy nose, runny nose</li><li>Mouth - <span class="qt1">itching</span>, swelling of the lips or tongue</li><li>Throat - <span class="qt1">itching</span>, tightness, trouble swallowing, swelling of the back of the throat</li><li>Chest - shortness of breath, coughing, wheezing, chest pain or tightness</li><li>Heart - weak pulse, passing out, shock</li><li>Gastrointestinal tract - vomiting, diarrhea, cramps</li><li>Nervous system - dizziness or fainting</li></ul><p>If someone is having a serious allergic reaction, call 911. If an auto-injector  is available, give the person the injection right away.</p></content>

    <document rank="4" url="https://medlineplus.gov/hemorrhoids.html">
      <content name="title">Hemorrhoids</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Hemorrhoidectomy</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Piles</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What are hemorrhoids?<p>Hemorrhoids are swollen, inflamed veins around your anus or the lower part of your rectum. There are two types:</p><ul><li>External hemorrhoids, which form under the skin around your anus</li><li>Internal hemorrhoids, which form in the lining of your anus and lower rectum</li></ul>What causes hemorrhoids?<p>Hemorrhoids happen when there is too much pressure on the veins around the anus. This can be caused by:</p><ul><li>Straining during bowel movements.</li><li>Sitting on the toilet for long periods of time.</li><li>Chronic constipation or diarrhea.</li><li>A low-fiber diet.</li><li>Weakening of the supporting tissues in your anus and rectum. This can happen with aging and pregnancy.</li><li>Frequently lifting heavy objects.</li></ul>What are the symptoms of hemorrhoids?<p>The symptoms of hemorrhoids depend on which type you have:</p><p>With external hemorrhoids, you may have:</p><ul><li>Anal <span class="qt1">itching</span></li><li>One or more hard, tender lumps near your anus</li><li>Anal pain, especially when sitting</li></ul><p>Too much straining, rubbing, or cleaning around your anus may make your symptoms worse. For many people, the symptoms of external hemorrhoids go away within a few days.</p><p>With internal hemorrhoids, you may have:</p><ul><li>Bleeding from your rectum - you would see bright red blood in your stool, on toilet paper, or in the toilet bowl after a bowel movement</li><li>Prolapse, which is a hemorrhoid that has fallen through your anal opening</li></ul><p>Internal hemorrhoids are usually not painful unless they are prolapsed. Prolapsed internal hemorrhoids may cause pain and discomfort.</p>How can I treat hemorrhoids at home?<p>You can most often treat your hemorrhoids at home by:</p><ul><li>Eating foods that are high in fiber.</li><li>Taking a stool softener or a fiber supplement.</li><li>Drinking enough fluids every day.</li><li>Not straining during bowel movements.</li><li>Not sitting on the toilet for long periods of time.</li><li>Taking over-the-counter pain relievers.</li><li>Taking warm baths several times a day to help relieve pain. This could be a regular bath or a sitz bath. With a sitz bath, you use a special plastic tub that allows you to sit in a few inches of warm water.</li><li>Using over-the-counter hemorrhoid creams, ointments, or suppositories to relieve mild pain, swelling, and <span class="qt1">itching</span> of external hemorrhoids.</li></ul>When do I need to see a health care provider for hemorrhoids?<p>You should see your health care provider if you:</p><ul><li>Still have symptoms after 1 week of at-home treatment.</li><li>Have bleeding from your rectum. Hemorrhoids are a common cause of bleeding, but other conditions can also cause bleeding. They include Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, colorectal cancer, and anal cancer. So it's important to see your provider to find the cause of the bleeding.</li></ul>How are hemorrhoids diagnosed?<p>To find out if you have hemorrhoids, your health care provider:</p><ul><li>Will ask about your medical history.</li><li>Will do a physical exam. Often providers can diagnose external hemorrhoids by looking at the area around your anus.</li><li>Will do a digital rectal exam to check for internal hemorrhoids. For this, the provider will insert a lubricated, gloved finger into the rectum to feel for anything that is abnormal.</li><li>May do procedures such as an anoscopy to check for internal hemorrhoids.</li></ul>What are the treatments for hemorrhoids?<p>If at-home treatments for hemorrhoids don't help you, you may need a medical procedure. There are several different procedures that your provider can do in the office. These procedures use different techniques to cause scar tissue to form in the hemorrhoids. This cuts off the blood supply, which usually shrinks the hemorrhoids. In severe cases, you may need surgery.</p>Can hemorrhoids be prevented?<p>You can help prevent hemorrhoids by:</p><ul><li>Eating foods that are high in fiber</li><li>Taking a stool softener or a fiber supplement</li><li>Drinking enough fluids every day</li><li>Not straining during bowel movements</li><li>Not sitting on the toilet for long periods of time</li></ul><p>NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases</p></content>
